value: seeds germinated in complete darkness. Germination under 12 h light/12 h dark against continuous dark, % at 15/5, 20/10, 25/15, 30/20, 35/25 C: 0.7 vs 0.0, 8.3 vs 6.0, 51.7 vs 33.5, 85.7 vs 64.2, 73.0 vs 53.2. method: seed germination under a 12 h light/12 h dark cycle against continuous darkness (dishes under two layers of aluminium foil) at five alternating day/night temperatures; Table 1 values for A. viridis alone

The Results text says 'Although lower germination was observed in the dark treatment, it was not an inhibiting factor'. Introduced-range populations only. value: GA3 sprayed on flowers cut germination of the resulting buried seeds from 98.0% (control) to 16.5% at 0.43 mM; 47.6% at 0.07 mM and 48.3% at 0.14 mM; at 0.28 mM the fall was marginal and the paper says this change was not significant. Bagging alone lowered germination by 24.6% (0.07 mM) and 31.5% (0.28 mM) against uncovered treated plants (no significant effect at 0.14 and 0.43 mM), and the control's bagging is not stated, so the fall cannot be credited to GA3 alone
method: GA3 (25, 50, 100, 150 mg/l = 0.07, 0.14, 0.28, 0.43 mM) sprayed to runoff on flowers in June, 2 to 4 days before flowering, after removal of terminal umbels; seeds from treated satellite umbels buried in peat boxes and scored for germination; TIBA and TIBA + IAA treatments in the same study
conditions: field plus buried-seed trial; one population near Vilnius, Lithuania (0.415 ha); 9 to 10 plants and 25 to 30 inflorescences treated; seeds collected late August 2016 to 2017 (the paper gives no year-by-year germination values); 100 seeds of each variant per box with at least three replications; boxes with peat buried about 10 cm from the beginning of October to April; sprayed inflorescences were covered with bags to exclude pollen-carrying insects, and distilled water was the control, but the paper does not say whether control inflorescences were bagged; covered against uncovered comparison on one part of the treated plants (Fig. 6); the 'bagging alone' figures compare covered with uncovered GA3-treated plants, and the paper's Methods ('sprayed inflorescences were covered') and Results ('one part of the treated plants were covered') differ on what was covered

value: germination in the dark was 22% against 56% in light; the paper's Methods contradict this: they say no germination was recorded in foil-wrapped dishes. The authors conclude from the dark result that both Ambrosia species require light for germination
method: germination in Petri dishes in light against dishes wrapped in aluminium foil to exclude light
conditions: laboratory growth chamber, 25/18 C with a 16 h day/8 h night cycle; 9 cm dishes on two layers of Whatman No. 1 paper moistened with tap water; seeds collected from open-field areas 2009 to 2014 and stored dry at 4 C; experiments repeated at least twice with five to six replicates, results combined as 10 to 12 replicates. Methods say 'No germination in Petri dishes wrapped with aluminum foil to prevent light penetration was recorded', hence all other experiments were in light; Results give 0.4% for A. confertiflora and 22% for A. artemisiifolia in the dark and 40% and 56% in light; the paper does not reconcile the two. The abstract states all three species germinate best in light from the soil surface. The quoted sentence names both A. confertiflora and A. artemisiifolia; this record takes only the A. artemisiifolia figure; no statistical test of light against dark is reported
